title: The hack that smuggles Substack past Twitter’s link ban
summary:
“I’m sick & tired of… having to share a screenshot and say ‘link in bio’ like a goddamn porn bot.” That’s @DefenderOfBasic on May 30, dropping a dead-simple workaround for Twitter’s link downranking: a Substack-proxy that re-hosts an article’s meta tags so Twitter thinks it’s “just another page” and renders a normal-looking card. The spiciest claim wasn’t even the tool—it was the swagger: “this cannot be banned… they can’t ban this without banning ALL external links,” because the code is forkable and the HTML can be recreated anywhere.

The arc: the long simmer is everyone complaining that Twitter punishes links (e.g., @danielbrottman’s Feb 27 “homies just want… a twitter dot com that doesn't punish posts for including links,” plus the ongoing “link in bio” clown show when links break). The trigger is Defender shipping the proxy + manifesto about internet resilience (“the internet cannot really be censored… as long as people know how to copy data and re-host it”). It peaks immediately as the replies turn into a celebratory mutual-aid bazaar—people like @Tangrenin ask how to tip because “this might help a number of people make more money,” @AskYatharth calls it a “support-mutuals-posting-links brigade,” and @eigenrobot declares “songs should be sung of this.”

Then Twitter adapts, and the thread evolves from “hack” to “cat-and-mouse”: on June 4 Defender notes Twitter can scan redirects and still downrank, so he adds “manual redirect mode” (no JS redirect; the human clicks a button). By late June, he’s flipped from outrage to game design: “substack” becomes a “guaranteed anti-viral keyword” you can use for containment. Why care: it’s a clean snapshot of users reasserting agency—turning platform punishment into a tool, and reminding everyone that on the web, copying + re-hosting is the nuclear option against feed-level censorship.
